246.title: The direct path
246.hook: a direct path for the purification of beings: four foundations of mindfulness (MN 10)
246.howItsDone: The Satipatthana Sutta is studied and practiced across the Buddhist world, especially in Theravada communities, where many meditation methods, including the Burmese insight traditions, trace themselves to it; the longer version is sometimes chanted in full.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your immeasurables, all four rooms in one sitting. Your line was immeasurable. Did you visit each room once? Day two hundred forty-six, and a new part of the path.

The word mindfulness is everywhere now. It's on apps, in office trainings, on the side of a tea box. Some of it traces back, one way or another, to an old text: a talk the Buddha is said to have given to the people of Kuru, in a market town called Kammasadhamma. For the next three weeks, we'll walk through it, section by section. It's long, and it repeats itself on purpose. Today: the opening line, and the map. Today's word: satipatthana.
screen: `MINDFULNESS, ON A TEA BOX.` → `ONE OLD TEXT.` → `THREE WEEKS, SECTION BY SECTION.`

segments.voice: The text is the Satipatthana Sutta, number ten in the Middle Length Discourses, with a longer twin, the Maha-satipatthana, in the Long Discourses. Sati means mindfulness, remembering to be present. Patthana is usually taken as foundation or establishing, though scholars argue about how to split the word. So: the establishing of mindfulness. It opens with a bold claim. The Buddha says this is the ekayana path, for the purification of beings, for getting past sorrow and lamentation, for the ending of pain and grief, for finding the true way, for realizing nibbana. Ekayana is a puzzle. Some older English translations said the only way. Others say the direct path, or the one-way path, a road that goes straight to one place. The word itself can bear several meanings, and teachers disagree. Then comes the map. There are four foundations, four places to set mindfulness down. The body. Feelings, meaning the pleasant, painful or neutral tone of experience. The mind, its states and moods. And dhammas, a hard word here, often translated mental qualities or phenomena: the patterns the Buddha taught people to recognize. One path, four doors into it. Every section of the sutta that follows fits somewhere on this map. For the next three weeks, when you get lost, come back to these four. Body, feelings, mind, dhammas.
screen: `SATI + PATTHANA: ESTABLISHING MINDFULNESS.` · `EKAYANA: ONLY, OR DIRECT?` · `BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, DHAMMAS.` · `ONE PATH, FOUR DOORS.` · then, large: `ONE WAY, FOUR DOORS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. We'll touch each door once. Body: feel where you're sitting, the weight, the contact. Feelings: is this moment pleasant, unpleasant, or neither? Mind: what's the mood right now, calm, restless, tired? Dhammas: is anything pulling at you, a want, an irritation, a doubt? Name the four quietly to yourself: body, feelings, mind, dhammas. Then just sit and let the breath be. The bell holds the time.
Satipatthana. The establishing of mindfulness, set down in four places: body, feelings, mind and dhammas.
Your line: one way, four doors. Today, try to say the four foundations from memory three times: body, feelings, mind, dhammas. Day two hundred forty-six.

the sutta has a longer twin in the Long Discourses
the Maha-satipatthana Sutta, DN 22.
'feelings' here means emotions like love or anger
it means the tone of experience: pleasant, painful or neither.

fork.setup: you're lost in a long text with many sections. what does the opening of the Satipatthana Sutta give you?
options: a list of rules.
a map: four foundations every section fits into.
a story about the Buddha's childhood.
fork.reveal: the opening sets out four foundations, body, feelings, mind and dhammas, and the rest of the sutta fills them in.

original.note: Pali satipaṭṭhāna: the establishing, or foundation, of mindfulness.

trapdoor: what you thought: satipatthana is just a long word for mindfulness.
what it means: mindfulness set down in four places: body, feelings, mind, dhammas.
what a scholar hears: the compound can split as sati + paṭṭhāna (foundation) or sati + upaṭṭhāna (establishing, being present); commentators and modern scholars read it both ways.

247.title: Ardent, aware, mindful
247.hook: the refrain: ardent, clearly knowing, mindful, putting aside longing and dismay (MN 10)
247.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions describe right effort with the image of a well-tuned lute, and the refrain 'ardent, clearly knowing, mindful' is often taught as a checklist for a good sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was satipatthana, the establishing of mindfulness. Your line: one way, four doors. Can you still name them? Body, feelings, mind, dhammas. Day two hundred forty-seven.

Heat is an odd thing to ask for in meditation. The usual picture of a meditator is cool: still water, a calm face, nothing burning. Yet when the Satipatthana Sutta describes someone practicing, the first quality it names is a kind of heat. And other texts set a warning right beside it. Too little fire, and nothing happens: you sit and drift. Too much, and you push until something breaks. The sutta has a refrain it repeats for every one of the four foundations, and its first word is about exactly this balance. Today's word: ardent.
screen: `HEAT, IN A TEXT ABOUT CALM?` → `TOO LITTLE, TOO MUCH.` → `THE REFRAIN'S FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: Every time the sutta introduces a foundation, it describes the one practicing with the same four phrases. Ardent. Clearly knowing. Mindful. Having put aside longing and dismay for the world. Take them one at a time. Ardent, in Pali atapi, comes from tapa, heat. It's the warmth of real interest, the fire that keeps you coming back. Clearly knowing, sampajano, means understanding what you're doing while you do it. Mindful, satima, is the one who remembers to stay present, who doesn't drift off. And the last phrase names what gets set aside: abhijjha and domanassa, wanting and discontent, the grab toward what we like and the sag of dismay at what we don't. So the refrain is a little portrait of a meditator. Warm, clear, present, and not pulled around. Why heat? Without it, mindfulness goes limp: you sit, and nothing happens, and you drift. Another text pairs it with gentleness, in a story about a monk named Sona. Before he was a monk, Sona had been skilled at the lute. He practiced walking meditation so hard his feet bled. The Buddha asked him about his lute. Were the strings too tight? It wouldn't play. Too loose? It wouldn't play either. Tuned just right, it sang. So ardent never means harsh. It means warm enough to stay, gentle enough to last.
screen: `ARDENT, CLEARLY KNOWING, MINDFUL.` · `ATAPI: FROM TAPA, HEAT.` · `SET ASIDE WANTING AND DISMAY.` · `SONA'S LUTE: NOT TOO TIGHT.` · then, large: `ARDENT AND GENTLE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and just watch whatever arises: breath, sounds, sensations. Bring a little warmth to it, real interest, as if this breath were worth noticing. Then check your grip. Is your jaw tight? Your forehead? Let them soften. Warm and soft at once. If you drift, come back without scolding. If you're straining, loosen one notch. Tune the string until it sings. The bell holds the time.
Ardent. Atapi, from the word for heat: the warm, steady interest that keeps mindfulness alive, never harsh.
Your line: ardent and gentle. Today, with one task you care about, check the string: too tight, too loose, or just right? Day two hundred forty-seven.

match.prompt: match each word of the refrain.

the Buddha's lute story says strings too tight won't play.

ardent, clearly knowing, mindful, having put aside longing and dismay.

fork.reveal: he asks Sona, a former musician, about his lute: the right tuning is neither too tight nor too loose. effort works the same way.

original.note: Pali ātāpī: ardent, from tapa, heat; the first word of the refrain.

trapdoor: what you thought: ardent means intense, pushing hard.
what it means: warm, steady interest, balanced by gentleness.
what a scholar hears: ātāpī shares its root with tapas, the ascetic 'heat' of Indian religion; the sutta keeps the warmth but, with Sona's lute, rejects strain.

248.title: The body: breathing
248.hook: gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, breathing in long, he knows it (MN 10)
248.howItsDone: Mindfulness of breathing (anapanasati) is among the most widely taught Buddhist meditations; practitioners sit upright and simply know each breath as long or short, then widen to the whole body and let it calm.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ardent, warm interest that never turns harsh. Your line was ardent and gentle. Did you check the tuning on anything? Day two hundred forty-eight, and the first foundation.

You've breathed about twenty thousand times since yesterday morning. You noticed maybe three of them: once climbing the stairs, once in a sigh, once when something scared you. The rest happened without you. The breath is the most faithful companion you have. It never takes a day off, and almost nobody pays it any attention. The Satipatthana Sutta starts its tour of the four foundations right here, with the body, and within the body, with the breath. Today: the body, breathing.
screen: `TWENTY THOUSAND BREATHS.` → `YOU NOTICED THREE.` → `THE FIRST FOUNDATION.`

segments.voice: The sutta sets the scene simply. A practitioner goes to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut. They sit down, legs crossed, body upright, and set mindfulness in front of them. Then the instruction. Breathing in long, they know, I breathe in long. Breathing out long, they know, I breathe out long. Breathing in short, they know, I breathe in short. Breathing out short, they know that too. Notice what isn't there. There's no command to breathe long. No counting, no special technique, no forcing. The breath does what it does, and the practitioner knows it. That's the whole first step: knowing. Then two more steps follow. They train themselves to breathe in and out experiencing the whole body. And they train themselves to breathe calming the body, letting the activity of the body settle. So the breath is both the thing you watch and the thing that slowly quiets you. A whole separate sutta, the Anapanasati Sutta, expands this into sixteen steps; the tradition calls the practice anapanasati, mindfulness of in-and-out breathing. Tradition also says it was the practice the Buddha himself used on the night of his awakening. Why start here? Because the breath is always available and always now. You can't breathe yesterday's breath. The moment you know this one, you've arrived in the body, and the other three doors are close by.
screen: `THE FOREST, THE TREE, THE EMPTY HUT.` · `BREATHING LONG, THEY KNOW IT.` · `NO FORCING, JUST KNOWING.` · `THE WHOLE BODY, THEN CALMING.` · then, large: `KNOWING THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, comfortable, as if at the root of a tree. Let the breath come in however it comes. If it's long, know it's long. If it's short, know it's short. Don't adjust it. After a few breaths, widen your attention to the whole body breathing: belly, chest, shoulders. Then let each out-breath soften something, just a little. Long, short, whole body, calming. The bell holds the time.
The body, breathing. The first foundation begins with the breath: long, short, the whole body, calming. No forcing, only knowing.
Your line: knowing the breath. Today, three times, catch one breath and know it: long or short. That's the whole assignment. Day two hundred forty-eight.

screen: `DAY 248 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TURNER AT THE LATHE.`

tradition says the Buddha used breath meditation on the night of his awakening
that's why many call it the Buddha's own practice.
a separate sutta expands breathing into sixteen steps
the Anapanasati Sutta.

options: breathe deeper right away.
know it: breathing in short, I know I breathe in short.
stop and try again later.
fork.reveal: the first step is only knowing. calming comes later, and it comes by itself, not by force.

original.note: Pali ānāpānasati: mindfulness of in-breathing and out-breathing.

trapdoor: what you thought: breath meditation means controlling the breath.
what it means: knowing the breath as it is, long or short, then letting the body calm.
what a scholar hears: 'calming the bodily formation' (passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ): the commentaries identify the bodily formation with the in-and-out breath itself.

249.title: The turner at the lathe
249.hook: as a skilled turner knows a long pull and a short pull (MN 10)
249.howItsDone: Teachers of mindfulness of breathing often use the sutta's image of the skilled turner to explain that the aim is plain, steady knowing of each breath, like a craftsperson's attention, rather than effortful control.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, breathing. Long, short, the whole body, calming. Your line was knowing the breath. Did you catch three breaths and know them? Day two hundred forty-nine.

Watch someone who's really good at a craft. A barber with the clippers. A baker shaping loaves. A carpenter planing a board. They aren't tense, and they aren't daydreaming either. Their hands know exactly what they're doing, stroke by stroke, and it looks almost easy. Right in the middle of the breathing instructions, the Satipatthana Sutta stops to give a picture like that. It's a workshop picture, from a craft most of us have never seen. Today: the turner at the lathe.
screen: `A BARBER, A BAKER, A CARPENTER.` → `HANDS THAT KNOW.` → `A WORKSHOP PICTURE.`

segments.voice: A turner is a woodworker who shapes wood on a lathe, spinning it while a blade carves it round: bowls, legs for a stool, beads. The sutta says it's like a skilled turner, or a turner's apprentice. Making a long turn, he knows, I make a long turn. Making a short turn, he knows, I make a short turn. In the same way, the one who meditates, breathing in long, knows I breathe in long; breathing in short, knows I breathe in short. The sutta doesn't describe the machine. It only says the turner knows each pull, long or short, as it happens. Long pull, short pull, all day long. So the picture has a rhythm, like the breath. Here's what the image adds. First, skill. The turner isn't straining to notice each pull; in skilled hands, the knowing is built in. Mindfulness of breathing is meant to become like that: a skill, not a strain. Second, the turner knows without stopping to comment. They don't say, what a lovely long pull, I'm so good at this. They just know it, and keep working. Third, the knowing is there for the sake of the work. A turner who lost track of the pull would ruin the bowl. The breath works the same way. Knowing it isn't an extra task on top of breathing. It's doing breathing well.
screen: `A TURNER SHAPES WOOD ON A LATHE.` · `LONG PULL, SHORT PULL.` · `KNOWING WITHOUT COMMENT.` · `A SKILL, NOT A STRAIN.` · then, large: `THE TURNER KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, hands resting. Let each breath be like a pull at the turner's lathe: a pull in, a pull out. Some pulls are long, some are short. Just know which is which, the way the turner's hands know, without comment and without changing the breath. Long. Short. Long. If a commentary starts up, let it go, and come back to the next pull. The bell holds the time.
The turner at the lathe. The skilled woodworker knows each long pull and each short pull; the meditator knows each breath the same way.
screen: `THE TURNER AT THE LATHE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the turner knows. Today, pick one thing you do with your hands, stirring, typing, folding, and know each stroke the way a turner would. Day two hundred forty-nine.

pairs: a long breath, known as long

right after long and short breaths, in MN 10.

the point is knowing without commentary, the way skilled hands work.

fork.reveal: the turner knows each pull without comment. the knowing serves the work; the commentary interrupts it.

what a scholar hears: the sutta's word is bhamakāra, a lathe-worker, and it names his apprentice too: the knowing is a skill that can be learned.

250.title: Inside and outside
250.hook: the refrain: in oneself, in others, both; arising and passing away (MN 10)
250.howItsDone: In insight meditation traditions, practitioners return to the sutta's refrain after each exercise: seeing the body, feelings and mind in themselves and in others, and watching them arise and pass away without clinging.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the turner at the lathe, knowing each pull without comment. Your line was the turner knows. Did your hands know one task well? Day two hundred fifty.

Some songs have a chorus that comes back after every verse, and by the end you're singing it without thinking. The Satipatthana Sutta works like that. After every single exercise, the breath, the postures, the parts of the body, feelings, the mind, all of it, the same few lines come back. It's easy to skip them as repetition. But some teachers call the chorus the heart of the whole sutta. The verses tell you where to look. The chorus tells you how. Today: inside and outside.
screen: `A CHORUS AFTER EVERY VERSE.` → `EASY TO SKIP.` → `THE VERSES SAY WHERE; THE CHORUS SAYS HOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the chorus, in plain words. The practitioner contemplates the body as a body internally, externally, and both internally and externally. They contemplate its nature of arising, its nature of passing away, and both arising and passing away. Or else mindfulness that there is a body is simply present, just enough for knowing and for continued mindfulness. And they live independent, not clinging to anything in the world. Take it in three pieces. Inside and outside. Internally means in yourself. Externally is usually explained as in others: the same breath, the same body, the same moods in the person across from you. Commentators and modern teachers read this line a few different ways, and the text doesn't settle it. One reading goes like this: what you learn in your own body helps you understand everyone else's. Next, arising and passing away. Whatever you watch, a breath, an itch, a mood, you see it come and you see it go. Watched closely, nothing in it holds still for long. This is the doorway to what Buddhists call impermanence, anicca, not as an idea, but as something you watch happen. Last, independent, not clinging. The knowing is just enough to know. It doesn't grab, doesn't build a story, doesn't need the breath to stay a certain way. Three moves, repeated after every exercise, until they become the way you look at everything.
screen: `THE CHORUS AFTER EVERY EXERCISE.` · `IN ONESELF, IN OTHERS, BOTH.` · `ARISING, PASSING AWAY.` · `JUST ENOUGH TO KNOW, CLINGING TO NOTHING.` · then, large: `IT ARISES, IT PASSES.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and pick one small sensation: the breath at the nostrils, warmth in the hands, a pressure where you sit. Watch it change. Notice it arise, shift, fade, arise again. Nothing in it holds still. Then, for a breath or two, remember that every person around you right now has a body doing the same. Inside, outside. Arising, passing. Just enough to know. The bell holds the time.
Inside and outside. The sutta's chorus: in yourself, in others, both, and always arising and passing away.
Your line: it arises, it passes. Today, pick one sensation, an itch, hunger, a tight shoulder, and watch it arise and pass instead of fighting it. Day two hundred fifty.

watching arising and passing is a doorway to impermanence
anicca, seen happening, not just thought about.

options: scratch it right away.
watch it rise, shift and fade, without grabbing or fighting.

fork.reveal: the chorus asks you to watch things come and go, knowing just enough to know, not clinging.

original.note: Pali anicca: impermanence, seen in the chorus as arising and passing away.

trapdoor: what you thought: inside and outside means paying attention to your body and your surroundings.
what it means: seeing body and mind in yourself, in others, and both, always arising and passing.

what a scholar hears: ajjhattaṃ/bahiddhā (internally/externally) is read by the commentaries as oneself and others, while some modern scholars suggest other readings; the text itself does not define the terms.

251.title: The body: postures
251.hook: walking, he knows he walks; standing, sitting, lying down (MN 10)
251.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay meditators often alternate sitting with walking meditation, pacing a short path slowly and knowing each step, and teachers encourage knowing the posture throughout the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: inside and outside, the chorus of the sutta. Your line was it arises, it passes. Did you watch one sensation come and go? Day two hundred fifty-one.
screen: `INSIDE AND OUTSIDE — IT ARISES, IT PASSES.`

segments.voice: Quick question, and don't move: how are you sitting right now? Legs crossed? One foot tucked under? Leaning on an elbow? A lot of people have to look down to find out. We spend the whole day in some position, standing in line, slumped on the couch, lying in bed scrolling, and we're almost never there for it. The body is in one place, and we're somewhere else entirely. The next exercise in the Satipatthana Sutta sounds almost too simple to count. Today: the body, postures.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU SITTING RIGHT NOW?` → `DID YOU HAVE TO LOOK?` → `ALMOST TOO SIMPLE.`

segments.voice: After the breath, the sutta turns to the four postures, in Pali the iriyapatha, the ways of moving. When walking, the practitioner knows, I am walking. When standing, they know, I am standing. When sitting, I am sitting. When lying down, I am lying down. And however the body is placed, they know it that way. That's the whole instruction. Then the chorus comes back: inside, outside, arising, passing, not clinging. It's tempting to laugh. Of course I know I'm sitting. But do you? Knowing it as a fact and knowing it as an experience are different. One is a thought about the body. The other is actually being in it: the weight on the seat, the feet on the floor, the slight lean. Why does this matter? Because the four postures cover your entire life. You are always in one of them. The breath gave you a doorway you can use anytime. The postures give you a second one, bigger and even harder to miss. You don't need a cushion or a quiet room. The checkout line is standing. The drive home is sitting. Falling asleep is lying down. There's a second gift, too. Walking meditation, used in many monasteries, draws on lines like this one. Monks and nuns walk slowly up and down a path, knowing each step. For some people, walking is easier than sitting still, and the sutta names walking right alongside sitting.
screen: `WALKING, STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN.` · `A FACT, OR AN EXPERIENCE?` · `ALWAYS IN ONE OF FOUR.` · `WALKING COUNTS TOO.` · then, large: `I KNOW I'M SITTING.`

segments.voice: Stay exactly how you are. Don't fix your posture first. Just know it. I am sitting, or standing, or lying down. Feel where the body touches something: the seat, the floor, the bed. Feel the shape you're making. Then, slowly, straighten a little, and know that too: I am straightening. Settle again. Rest in the plain knowing of the posture. The bell holds the time.
The body, postures. Walking, standing, sitting, lying down: in whatever way the body is placed, know it that way.
Your line: I know I'm sitting. Today, once an hour if you can, name your posture to yourself and feel it for one breath. Day two hundred fifty-one.

match.prompt: match each posture to where it shows up.

walking, standing, sitting and lying down are all named.
knowing you're sitting is the same as thinking 'I'm sitting'
the practice is feeling the posture, not just knowing it as a fact.
you must fix your posture before you can know it
the sutta says: however the body is placed, know it that way.

options: sit up straight first; slumping doesn't count.
know it: however the body is placed, know it that way.

original.note: Pali iriyāpatha: the postures, literally the ways of moving.

trapdoor: what you thought: knowing your posture is too simple to be a practice.
what it means: feeling the body as it is, in every position, all day.

what a scholar hears: the commentary on this passage asks how this differs from a dog knowing it walks, and answers that the practitioner knows it without the idea of a lasting self doing the walking.

252.title: The body: clear knowing
252.hook: going and returning, looking, bending, dressing, eating, even in the toilet (MN 10)
252.howItsDone: In many monasteries, clear knowing is practiced through daily chores, eating in silence, and slow, deliberate movement; lay practitioners often choose one routine act, like washing dishes, as a daily reminder.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, postures. Your line was I know I'm sitting. How many hours did you catch yourself? Day two hundred fifty-two, the end of the first week in the sutta.

Getting dressed. Chewing your food. Going to the toilet. These aren't the parts of the day anyone expects to hear about in a teaching on awakening. The Satipatthana Sutta lists them anyway, right there in its instructions, next to walking, sitting and falling asleep. There's no special room for this practice, and no special hour. It isn't being crude. It's making a point: there is no part of the day that doesn't count. Today's word: sampajanna, clear knowing.
screen: `DRESSING, CHEWING, THE TOILET.` → `RIGHT IN THE INSTRUCTIONS.` → `NO PART OF THE DAY LEFT OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the list, in plain words. The practitioner acts with clear knowing when going forward and coming back. When looking ahead and looking away. When bending and stretching a limb. When wearing the robe and carrying the bowl. When eating, drinking, chewing and tasting. When relieving themselves. When walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking, and staying silent. Sampajanna means clear knowing, or full awareness: knowing what you're doing, and why, while you do it. It's the second word of the refrain you met five days ago, now given a whole section of its own. The commentaries later unpacked it into four kinds: knowing the purpose of an action, knowing whether it's suitable, keeping it within the range of practice, and seeing it without the idea of a solid self behind it. You don't have to remember all four. The simple version is enough: you're there for it. Look back over this week and you'll see the path widening. Satipatthana: one way, four doors. Ardent and gentle. The breath, known long and short, like the turner at the lathe. The chorus: inside and outside, arising and passing. The postures, the whole shape of the body. And now clear knowing, the smallest actions of an ordinary day. The breath was one thread. The postures were four. This is everything else.
screen: `GOING, LOOKING, BENDING, DRESSING, EATING.` · `EVEN IN THE TOILET.` · `SAMPAJANNA: KNOWING WHAT AND WHY.` · `THE WEEK: FROM BREATH TO EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `EVEN THIS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Slowly raise one hand, and know it rising. Turn the palm over, and know it turning. Lower it, and know it lowering. Now turn your head a little to one side: know the looking. Back to center. Bend a finger, stretch it. Each small movement, known while it happens. Then rest your hands and just sit, knowing you're sitting. The bell holds the time.
Sampajanna. Clear knowing: being there for the smallest actions of the day, from getting dressed to eating to the toilet.
Your line: even this. Today, do one ordinary chore, washing a dish, brushing your teeth, tying your shoes, with clear knowing from start to finish. Day two hundred fifty-two.

original.note: Pali sampajañña: clear knowing, full awareness of what you're doing and why.

trapdoor: what you thought: clear knowing is a special meditative state.
what it means: being there for ordinary actions, knowing what you do and why.
what a scholar hears: sampajañña is from sam + pa + jānāti, 'to know thoroughly'; the commentary's four kinds (purpose, suitability, domain, non-delusion) come from Buddhaghosa, not the sutta itself.
